# Learning Qt, and working with AI {#sec-learning}

Qt is large, it changes every release, and most of what the internet knows about it is out of
date. This last chapter is about learning it efficiently and about using AI assistants
without being misled by them.

## Concepts you own, details you look up {#sec-own-concepts}

Some things you must understand yourself: what a binding does, why the event loop must not
block, who owns an object. Without them you cannot tell a good answer from a plausible one,
whether it comes from a colleague, a forum or an AI.

Other things nobody memorizes: the argument order of a function, the name of an option. Look
them up, every time. This guide teaches the first kind and links to the second.

## Read in the right order {#sec-reading}

When you meet a new Qt module, spend fifteen minutes in this order:

1. The module's overview page: what problem it solves, which classes matter.
2. One example, end to end.
3. The reference pages of the two or three classes that example used.
4. Now write your own code.

Qt's own examples and tests show current, working usage. When the documentation leaves a
question open, the test suite of that class often answers it.

## Recognize stale Qt {#sec-stale-qt}

Most Qt code online, and in the data AI models learned from, is Qt 5. It often still
compiles, but it is not how Qt 6 works. Learn its tells:

| Qt 5 | Qt 6 |
|---|---|
| `qmake` and `.pro` files | CMake with `qt_add_qml_module()` |
| `qmlRegisterType<T>("Uri", 1, 0, "T")` | `QML_ELEMENT` in the class |
| `setContextProperty("name", &object)` | required properties (@sec-required) |
| `connect(a, SIGNAL(x()), b, SLOT(y()))` | `connect(a, &A::x, b, &B::y)` |
| `import QtQuick 2.15` | `import QtQuick` |
| `onClicked: ...` inside `Connections` | `function onClicked() { ... }` inside `Connections` |

When an answer contains one of these, check it against the Qt 6 documentation before you use
it.

## Give the AI current Qt knowledge {#sec-agent-skills}

A coding agent repeats what it learned unless it gets better context. The Qt Company
publishes **agent skills** for the common AI coding tools. They correct the known mistakes
and add Qt-specific workflows:

| Skill | What it does |
|---|---|
| `qt-qml` | QML best practices; corrects typical mistakes with bindings, scoping, modules and types |
| `qt-cmake-project` | Qt 6 CMake projects; corrects qmake habits and old `qt5_*` macros |
| `qt-qml-review`, `qt-cpp-review` | code review with linters plus deeper analysis |
| `qt-qml-test` | writes Qt Quick Test cases for a component |
| `qt-ui-design` | layout, navigation and UX review |

The same repository provides a **Qt documentation server** (an MCP server) that lets the
agent look up the current API instead of guessing it.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Qt agent skills](https://github.com/TheQtCompanyRnD/agent-skills)
:::

## Let the tools judge the result {#sec-tools-judge}

An agent is only as good as the feedback it gets. Compiler warnings, qmllint, tests and
sanitizers give it ground truth instead of its own confidence. A project where one command
runs every check is a project an agent can work in:

```sh
cmake --workflow --preset dev                 # build and run every test
cmake --build --preset dev --target check     # every linter
```

The quality gates of @sec-quality and the tests of @sec-testing are the same gates you want
for human contributors. For UI work, a live preview (Qt offers one as an MCP tool) lets the
agent see a change instead of describing it.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [QML Live Preview MCP tool](https://www.qt.io/blog/introducing-the-qml-live-preview-mcp-tool-for-agentic-development-of-embedded-devices)
:::

## Own what you ship {#sec-own}

Review generated code the way you would review a colleague's: read every line, run it, test
it. Keep only what you can explain.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
If you could not rewrite it from scratch with an hour and the documentation, you do not
understand it yet. Go back to the concept.
:::
